description: High school builders taking on the Astronaut Health Monitoring challenge. I’ve built predictive ML models for Parkinson’s research, do FTC robotics (CAD + hardware), and and doing genomic research. Our goal, a real-time vitals dashboard that flags health risks early using NASA data.
summary: On a Mars mission, a question to Earth and its answer can be many minutes apart, so astronauts must notice changes in their own health and decide what to do alone. Health Copilot is an offline web app that learns each astronaut's personal baseline from pre-flight data, detects gradual drift across 13 health indicators, and explains every flag in plain language. A transparent five-level decision table then gives a clear next step, from "monitor" to "contact flight surgeon", and writes a compact report for Earth that shows the signal delay. A drift map shows all indicators over the mission at a glance, and a daily check-in adds a reaction-time test and self-ratings. The app also reads real solar storm events from NASA's DONKI database. The astronaut never gets an alarm without a reason and an action. All crew health data is simulated; this is a decision-support prototype, not a medical device.
details:
WHAT IT DOES - Health Copilot is an offline web app that helps astronauts on a Mars mission evaluate and act on their own health when a doctor on Earth is minutes away. It runs entirely on the astronaut's device, with no server. Screens: Today (status and daily check-in), Drift map (every indicator over the mission), Alert (why it fired and what to do), Earth (signal delay and a report for mission control), and Crew (triage level per person, radiation dose, space weather).

HOW IT WORKS - 1. Personal baseline: the mean and standard deviation of 30 pre-flight days, for each astronaut and each of 13 indicators (heart rate variability, resting heart rate, SpO2, sleep duration and efficiency, reaction time and lapses, mood, fatigue, stress, exercise, skin temperature, body mass). Nobody is compared with a population average. 2. Drift detection: each day's value becomes a z-score against the personal baseline, smoothed with an exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA). This catches small shifts sustained over days that a fixed threshold misses. Fixed safety limits (SpO2 below 92%, resting heart rate above 100 bpm, skin temperature 1.5 °C above baseline) act as a backstop. 3. Triage: a five-row decision table returns one of five levels (nominal, monitor, repeat measurement, self-care action, contact flight surgeon) based on how many indicators are flagged, for how long, and across which body systems. The rule that fired is shown on screen. 4. Daily check-in: a 30-second reaction-time test (a lapse is a response of 500 ms or slower) plus mood, fatigue and stress ratings feed the same system. 5. Earth report: a plain-text summary under 1 kB, written to be understood without a follow-up question. An orbital model of an Earth-to-Mars transfer computes the signal delay: 4 min 13 s one way on mission day 140, rising to about 12.5 min by day 250.

DEMO SCENARIO - Press "Play tour". On day 137 the app starts watching Flight Engineer Chen. By day 140 her HRV is 26% below her baseline and her reaction lapses have risen about fourfold, along with shorter, less efficient sleep. The app recommends a sleep and light schedule change and a repeat test, three days before her own fatigue rating leaves its normal range. She follows the plan and the trend is recovering by day 143.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT - It supports crew autonomy when real-time medical support is impossible. It is explainable: every alert states the numbers behind it and the rule that fired. It is conservative: it never diagnoses, and it separates "watch this" from "act on this" to avoid alarm fatigue. The same approach could serve other isolated crews, such as Antarctic stations or submarines.

WHAT IS CREATIVE - Personal baselines instead of population thresholds. - A drift map and a ridge model that show multi-signal drift at a glance. - Signal delay computed from an orbital model rather than a fixed number. - A report written for a one-way conversation. DATA Real NASA data: solar flare and solar energetic particle events from NASA's DONKI database, shown in the Crew view. Published values: cruise radiation of 1.84 mSv/day (Mars Science Laboratory RAD, Zeitlin et al. 2013) and the 600 mSv career limit (NASA-STD-3001). All crew health data is simulated: a fictional 4-person crew over 30 pre-flight days and a 250-day transit. Baseline values and scenario sizes are illustrative, not taken from spaceflight datasets.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED - Privacy: the crew view shows triage level only, and self-ratings stay on the device unless the astronaut sends them. - Works fully offline. - Accessibility: status uses icons and labels, not colour alone, and the app works on phones and desktops. - Honesty about limits: thresholds and guidance are not clinically validated. A flight version would need real wearable data, in-flight re-baselining and protocols approved by flight surgeons.

TOOLS - HTML, CSS and JavaScript in a single file, canvas and SVG charts, browser local storage, and GitHub Pages hosting. No frameworks or external libraries. The code and written materials were produced with an AI assistant (Claude, by Anthropic) under our team's direction; this is acknowledged in the code and the README.
